newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen ends higher on yen swap rate falls.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen ends higher on yen swap rate falls.

text.p: The key March Euroyen contract on the TIFFE ended firmer on Monday in response to falls in yen interest rate swaps (IRS) due to aggressive buying of fixed interest rates for floating rates by city and long-term banks, traders said.
"Major long-term and city banks received fixed interest rates in various maturities (in the swap market), inducing hedge purchases in the euroyen market," said a bank trader.
Most purchases of fixed rates appeared to have been prompted by banks' need for asset and liability management for their portfolios.
The March rose to around 98.92 in response to swap rate falls, compared with Friday's 98.86 settlement. It ended at 98.89.
But profit-taking selling in the March set in at over 98.90, making its topside limited, traders said.
The key three-year IRS was at 1.50/54 percent, down from Friday's 1.53/57 percent.
"I don't know how long such buying (of fixed rates) will last given that recent economic data shows that the economy is still on a recovery track," said another city bank trader.
But he added that developments in a recent financial market scandal may force the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to provide ample liquidity to alleviate possible upward pressure on rates.

A local news agency on Monday quoted a lawyer for Ryuichi Koike, a key figure in the high-profile payoff scandal involving Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd and Nomura Securities Co Ltd as saying that securities firms Nikko and Daiwa had also conducted illegal deals for him.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank and Nomura Securities, both of which had leading shares in the Japanese government bond (JGB) underwriting syndicate, have been suspended from participating in JGB auctions.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) drained 300 billion yen from the money market through its regular operation at 0020 GMT, leaving the market with a 270 billion yen surplus.
The central bank has been providing ample liquidity to the market in a bid to offset upward pressure on rates typically seen at the end of the month, traders said.
